newsitem.title: GERMANY: German govt, industry see Europe on track for EMU.
newsitem.headline: German govt, industry see Europe on track for EMU.

text.p: German Chancellor Helmut Kohl and leading industrialists on Monday insisted European economic and monetary union (EMU) would start punctually in 1999, even as an opposition leader sparks a new row over monetary union.

While much of the German public remained unconvinced about the benefits of a single European currency, Kohl and industry leaders said they were confident European Union leaders had set a reliable framework for monetary union.

In an article to appear in the economic daily Handelsblatt on Tuesday, Kohl wrote that decisions made at the EU summit in Dublin earlier this month "ensure that European monetary union can begin punctually on January 1, 1999."
"The goal is to begin with as many participants as possible," he added. Of course, the door will remain wide open for all who qualify later."

Kohl's insistence that all was well on the road to Europe's single currency came on the heels of evidence that the German public was still wary of giving up their Deutschmark for the euro and opposition warnings about the costs of EMU.
Seperately, Germany's Foreign Minister Klaus Kinkel urged Britain to make a choice on whether it wants closer integration with the EU.
Britain must hold a general election by next May and Europe is a key issue for Prime Minister John Major's Conservatives and the opposition Labour Party.

Gerhard Schroeder, premier of Lower Saxony and a prime SPD contender to challenge Kohl in 1998 elections, said in an interview in the newsweekly Focus that "naturally the euro will be weaker than the mark".

He also stirred fears that Germany would end up supporting weaker European countries after the euro is introduced in the same way that west Germany was forced to transfer billions each year to support east Germany following 1990 unification.
Schroeder was briskly attacked as a "populist" by members of the government and a leading member of his own party, but a recent poll showed that many Germans shared his doubts.

A poll by the INRA institute found 54 percent of Germans surveyed felt the euro would bring them disadvantages while only 30 percent saw benefits. Other surveys found about two-thirds of Germans opposed the European currency.
German Finance Minister Theo Waigel, rejecting criticism of the European currency, said the single market and common currency were in German interests.
"They create a zone of stability that guarantee our country peace, prosperity and jobs in the 21st century," he said.
Hoping to convince a wary public on the virtues of EMU, Germany has stuck to a hard line interpretation of the fiscal restrictions on budget deficits and debt.

It carried out a controversial but successful campaign this year to gain EU backing for a "stability pact" that would impose penalties against EMU participants who met the criteria in order to participate join EMU, but later relaxed discipline.

German industry leaders, in statements to appear in Handelsblatt on Tuesday, appeared satisfied with the results achieved in Dublin and were confident that enough EU member states would qualify for EMU to ensure its start in 1999.

Commerzbank AG chairman Martin Kohlhaussen said the EMU framework instilled confidence and that the first EMU participants would probably be Germany, France, Belgium, the Netherlands, Luxembourg, Austria, Ireland and Finland.
The decision about which countries would be eligible to join the EMU in 1999 will be made in 1998 and based on data from 1997 budget and economic performance.
Yves Thibault de Silguy, European Commissioner for Economics and Finance, said in a statement for Handelsblatt that all EU member states were committed to the EMU criteria.
"The markets today are convinced that there will be a euro and it will be a stable currency. One gains the confidence of the market only slowly, but loses it quickly," he warned.
-- Bonn Newsroom, 49 228 26097150
